title: Why separate the scheduler (decides WHEN, atomically claims a job `SCHEDULED → QUEUED`) from workers (decide HOW) via a queue, and how do you handle worker crashes (visibility timeout / lease), retries (backoff + jitter → DLQ), cancellation (final state check), and hot time-buckets (shard by `hash(jobId) % N`)?
shortTitle: Why separate the scheduler from the workers, and how do you handle failures?

s1_definition.profdef: Separating the scheduler from the workers is a separation of concerns where the scheduler owns the timing decision — it decides when a job is due and atomically moves it from SCHEDULED to QUEUED, placing it on a queue — while the workers own the execution decision — they pull from the queue and decide how to perform the work. Connecting them through a queue decouples the two so they scale, deploy, and fail independently, and it smooths bursts because the queue buffers work the workers consume at their own pace. Worker crashes are handled with a visibility timeout or lease, meaning a claimed job becomes invisible to other workers for a bounded time and reappears for re-delivery if the worker dies before acknowledging, so no job is lost. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and, after a maximum number of attempts, route the job to a dead-letter queue for investigation rather than retrying forever. Cancellation is honored by checking the job's current state just before executing, so a job cancelled after being queued is skipped. Hot time-buckets, where one moment has far too many due jobs, are spread by sharding the bucket across N partitions using the hash of the job id modulo N so the load distributes across workers.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine two distinct roles. The scheduling clerk watches the clock and the calendar; the moment a task is due, he stamps it "ready" and drops it into the out-tray — he never does the task himself, he only decides when. The processing clerks pick tasks from the out-tray whenever they are free and actually do the work. The out-tray between them is the queue, and because of it the scheduling clerk never waits for a processing clerk, and you can add more processing clerks on a busy day without touching the scheduler. If a processing clerk faints mid-task, the task was only "on loan" to him for a set time, so after that time it reappears in the tray for someone else (visibility timeout). If a task keeps failing, it is retried a few times with growing pauses, then set aside in a special problem tray for a supervisor (dead-letter queue). Before starting any task a clerk double-checks it was not cancelled meanwhile. And when one minute has a flood of tasks, the bank opens several numbered trays and routes each task to a tray by a simple rule so no single tray overflows.
s1_definition.oneliner: The scheduler decides when and atomically moves a job from SCHEDULED to QUEUED on a queue, workers decide how and consume from it, and a visibility timeout recovers crashed workers, backoff-with-jitter plus a dead-letter queue bounds retries, a pre-execution state check honors cancellation, and sharding a hot bucket by hash of the job id spreads the load.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine two distinct roles. The scheduling clerk watches the clock and the calendar; the moment a task is due, he stamps it "ready" and drops it into the out-tray — he never does the task himself, he only decides when. The processing clerks pick tasks from the out-tray whenever they are free and actually do the work. The out-tray between them is the queue, and because of it the scheduling clerk never waits for a processing clerk, and you can add more processing clerks on a busy day without touching the scheduler. If a task keeps failing, it is retried a few times with growing pauses, then set aside in a special problem tray for a supervisor (dead-letter queue). Before starting any task a clerk double-checks it was not cancelled meanwhile. And when one minute has a flood of tasks, the bank opens several numbered trays and routes each task to a tray by a simple rule so no single tray overflows.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason to separate the scheduler from the workers is that "when to run" and "how to run" are genuinely different responsibilities with different scaling and failure characteristics. The scheduler is lightweight and timing-focused: it repeatedly finds due jobs and enqueues them, and there is usually only a small number of scheduler instances (often one active with standbys) to keep the timing decision simple and avoid duplicate scheduling. The workers are the heavy, variable part: the actual work might call external systems, take seconds, and need many parallel instances, and you want to scale them up and down with load without affecting the timing logic. A queue between them decouples their pace entirely — the scheduler enqueues at the rate jobs become due, and the workers dequeue at the rate they can process, with the queue absorbing the difference. This also isolates failure: a worker crash does not stop the scheduler, and a scheduler restart does not lose in-flight work sitting on the queue.

The atomic SCHEDULED to QUEUED transition is critical to correctness. When the scheduler finds a due job, it must move it out of the "to be scheduled" structure and onto the queue in one indivisible step, so that if two scheduler instances run or the scheduler retries, the job is enqueued exactly once and not left half-moved. In a Redis-based design this is a Lua script that reads the due job from the sorted set and pushes it to the queue list, removing it from the sorted set, all atomically. In a database design it is a transaction that updates the row's status to QUEUED and inserts a queue record, or uses select-for-update-skip-locked so each scheduler instance claims distinct jobs. The guarantee you want is that a job is never scheduled twice and never silently dropped during the transition.

Worker crashes are handled with a visibility timeout, also called a lease. When a worker pulls a job from the queue, the job is not deleted immediately; instead it becomes invisible to other workers for a lease duration while that worker processes it. If the worker finishes and acknowledges, the job is removed for good. But if the worker crashes before acknowledging, the lease expires, the job becomes visible again, and another worker picks it up. This is how systems like SQS and Redis-based queues guarantee at-least-once delivery without losing work on a crash. The lease must be longer than the expected processing time, and long-running jobs must extend the lease (heartbeat) so they are not re-delivered while still running. The consequence of at-least-once delivery is that a job may run more than once on a crash, so the work itself must be idempotent — processing the same job twice must not double-charge an account.

Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum attempt count feeding a dead-letter queue. When a job fails, you do not retry immediately and forever, because an immediate retry often hits the same transient problem and retrying forever hides real failures. Instead you re-enqueue the job with a delay that grows exponentially with the attempt number, and you add random jitter so that many jobs that failed together do not all retry at the same instant and overwhelm the dependency (the thundering herd). After a configured maximum number of attempts, you stop retrying and move the job to a dead-letter queue, a separate queue where failed jobs accumulate for a human or an automated process to inspect, so a permanently broken job neither disappears nor loops forever. For example attempt one retries after a base delay, attempt two after roughly double, attempt three after roughly quadruple, each plus a small random offset, and after the fifth failure the job lands in the dead-letter queue.

Cancellation is honored with a final state check just before execution. Because a job may sit on the queue for a while between being scheduled and being executed, it can be cancelled in that window. A worker, before doing the actual work, re-reads the job's authoritative current state (from the database or the job store), and if it is now CANCELLED it skips execution and acknowledges the message so it leaves the queue. This "check the final state at the last moment" pattern avoids executing work that is no longer wanted, and it is important because the queue itself usually cannot un-enqueue a specific message, so the cancellation signal lives in the job's state and the worker consults it.

Hot time-buckets are handled by sharding. If jobs are organized into time buckets (for example per minute), a single very popular minute — say, midnight when millions of daily tasks are scheduled — can concentrate a huge number of due jobs onto one bucket key and one scheduler path, creating a bottleneck. You spread this by partitioning each bucket into N shards and assigning each job to a shard by hashing its job id modulo N, for example `jobs:2026-10-24T00:00:shard-<hash(jobId) % N>`. Then N scheduler workers each drain one shard in parallel, distributing the storage and the enqueue load evenly. The hash ensures a given job always lands in the same shard (so it is found and not duplicated) while the overall distribution is even. This is the same consistent-partitioning idea used throughout distributed systems to avoid hotspots.

A senior nuance is that the whole design assumes idempotent workers because of at-least-once delivery, so you design jobs around an idempotency key and a processed-jobs record, skipping a job whose id you have already completed. Another nuance is observability: you track queue depth, job age (time from due to executed), retry counts, and dead-letter volume, because a growing queue depth means workers are under-provisioned, a rising job age means you are missing deadlines, and a filling dead-letter queue means something is systematically failing. A final nuance is ordering: a plain queue does not guarantee strict ordering across shards, so if some jobs for the same entity must run in order, you route them to the same shard (by the entity id) so their relative order is preserved within that shard.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs the delayed-job platform and must make it robust against worker crashes, failures, cancellations, and midnight hot-spots.

Problem 1 — The scheduler and workers were one process, so a slow worker blocked timing and scaling workers meant redeploying the scheduler. Splitting them through a queue fixed this. This is the scheduler-worker separation.

Problem 2 — A worker crashed mid-job and the job vanished. Adding a visibility timeout meant the job reappeared for another worker after the lease expired. This is crash recovery via lease.

Problem 3 — A flaky downstream caused jobs to fail, and naive immediate retries hammered it; and a user cancelled a reminder that still fired. Adding backoff-with-jitter plus a dead-letter queue, and a pre-execution cancellation check, fixed both. Plus midnight concentrated millions of jobs on one bucket, fixed by sharding by hash of the job id.

We will model a scheduler that atomically moves due jobs from SCHEDULED to QUEUED on a queue, workers that lease jobs with a visibility timeout and re-deliver on crash, retry with backoff-jitter into a dead-letter queue, check cancellation before executing, and shard a hot bucket by hash modulo N.

The code will have a `Job` with a state, a `JobQueue` with lease-based claim and visibility-timeout re-delivery, a `Scheduler` doing the atomic SCHEDULED-to-QUEUED move with bucket sharding, a `Worker` with cancellation check and retry-to-DLQ, and a demo exercising crash, retry, cancellation, and sharding.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: several jobs scheduled into the queue, plus a crash, a persistently failing job, and a cancelled job.

Step 1 — The scheduler takes each due job, computes its shard as the hash of its id modulo four so that a busy minute spreads across four partitions, and atomically moves it from SCHEDULED to QUEUED by placing it on the queue. The scheduler only decided timing and placement; it never executed anything.

Step 2 — A worker claims the first reminder. Claiming leases it, making it invisible to other workers for the visibility timeout, so no second worker can grab the same job. The worker runs it, it succeeds, and the worker acknowledges, which removes it from the queue for good.

Step 3 — To simulate a crash, a worker leases a job and then dies before acknowledging. The job is not lost; it sits in the leased set with a lease expiry. When time advances past the lease, the queue returns it to the ready set, and another worker re-claims and processes it. This is at-least-once delivery via visibility timeout.

Step 4 — A persistently failing job is claimed and fails. Instead of retrying instantly or forever, the queue re-enqueues it with an exponentially growing delay plus random jitter, incrementing the attempt count each time. After the fifth attempt it stops and moves the job to the dead-letter queue, where it waits for investigation rather than looping forever.

Step 5 — A reminder is scheduled and then cancelled by the user while it sits queued. When a worker claims it, before doing any work it checks the job's authoritative state, sees CANCELLED, skips execution, and acknowledges so the job leaves the queue cleanly. No unwanted reminder is sent.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I separate the scheduler from the workers because deciding when a job runs and deciding how it runs are genuinely different responsibilities with different scaling and failure needs. The scheduler is lightweight and timing-focused, usually one active instance with standbys to keep timing simple, and it repeatedly finds due jobs and atomically moves each from SCHEDULED to QUEUED on a queue. The workers are the heavy, variable part that calls external systems and needs many parallel instances, and they consume from the queue at their own pace. The queue between them decouples their rates and isolates failure, so a worker crash never stops the scheduler and a scheduler restart never loses work already on the queue.

The atomic SCHEDULED-to-QUEUED transition matters for correctness, because the job must move out of the to-be-scheduled structure and onto the queue in one indivisible step, so even if the scheduler retries or runs twice the job is enqueued exactly once and never left half-moved. In Redis that is a Lua script; in a database it is a transaction or select-for-update-skip-locked.

I handle worker crashes with a visibility timeout, also called a lease. When a worker claims a job it is not deleted but made invisible to other workers for the lease duration, and if the worker acknowledges it is removed for good, but if the worker crashes before acknowledging the lease expires and the job is re-delivered to another worker. That gives at-least-once delivery, which means a job can run more than once on a crash, so I make the work itself idempotent with an idempotency key and a processed-jobs record. I handle retries with exponential backoff and jitter so failed jobs do not retry instantly or in lockstep and overwhelm a struggling dependency, and after a maximum attempt count I route the job to a dead-letter queue so a permanently broken job neither loops forever nor disappears, but waits for investigation.

I honor cancellation with a final state check: because a job can sit queued for a while, it may be cancelled in that window, so a worker re-reads the job's authoritative state just before executing, and if it is now cancelled it skips the work and acknowledges the message. And I handle hot time-buckets — like midnight when millions of daily jobs come due at once — by sharding each bucket across N partitions using the hash of the job id modulo N, so N scheduler workers drain the shards in parallel and no single key or worker is a bottleneck, while a given job always lands in the same shard so it is never duplicated.

In my banking platform I built exactly this for reminders, settlement retries, and hold expirations. Splitting scheduler from workers let me scale workers for load without touching timing, the visibility timeout recovered jobs from crashed workers, backoff-with-jitter plus a dead-letter queue tamed a flaky downstream, the pre-execution cancellation check stopped reminders that users had cancelled, and sharding by hash of the job id spread the midnight flood evenly. The nuances I always mention are that the design assumes idempotent workers, that I watch queue depth, job age, retry counts, and dead-letter volume as the key health signals, and that when some jobs for the same entity must run in order I route them to the same shard to preserve their relative order.
